title: fix: guard against NaN/float in gas oracle BigInt conversion
description:
> Oracle guards now catch the NaN,
> Math.round tames the float,
> gas price errors handled with grace,
> no more BigInt bloat.

## What it solves

The gas oracle parsing in `useDefaultGasPrice` crashes with "The number NaN cannot be converted to a BigInt" when oracle responses contain undefined/invalid values, or when floating-point multiplication produces non-integer results before `BigInt()` conversion. This causes repeated console errors every 20 seconds during gas price polling.

Related: [WA-1920](https://linear.app/safe-global/issue/WA-1920/twap-order-flow-glitches-on-web-with-pending-signer) — this fix addresses the NaN console errors observed during investigation, but does not resolve the UI flickering issue itself.

## How this PR fixes it

Adds `Number.isFinite()` validation before `BigInt()` conversion and `Math.round()` to handle floating-point precision in both Etherscan and non-Etherscan oracle parsing paths. Invalid values now throw descriptive errors that flow through the existing oracle fallback chain (try next oracle → try fixed config → surface error to hook consumer) instead of crashing with an opaque TypeError.

Also adds a comprehensive test suite for `useDefaultGasPrice` (27 tests) since none existed previously.

## How to test it

1. Run the new tests: `cd packages/utils && npx jest --testPathPattern='useDefaultGasPrice' --no-watchman`
2. Run the existing web gas price tests: `cd apps/web && npx jest --testPathPattern='useGasPrice' --no-watchman`
3. Verify gas fee estimation works on the transaction confirmation screen (any chain)

## Visual summary

flowchart LR

    B -->|Yes| C[Math.round + BigInt]
    B -->|No / NaN / Infinity| D[Throw descriptive error]

findings.claim: A stale TODO comment ("use log Error here") with commented-out code remains in the file.

The isFinite guard only rejects non-numeric values, so inputs like null, an empty string, or "0" from an oracle are silently converted to 0n rather than triggering a fallback to the next oracle, and if suggestBaseFee exceeds FastGasPrice the computed priority fee can come out negative without being caught; downstream code checks for null/undefined but not for zero or negative values.
Once the guard is fixed to reject empty/null values, tests should be added for those inputs asserting either an error is thrown or a fallback to the next oracle occurs.

The value parsing should go through a guarded helper that rejects null/undefined, trims strings, treats '' as invalid, checks Number.isFinite, and requires the result to be greater than 0 (or >= 0 for the base fee), throwing otherwise so the next-oracle fallback executes.

Extracting the numeric parsing into an exported pure helper and unit-testing it directly would make it cheaper to cover the rounding and empty/null-input cases and would remove the need for waitFor in those tests.
The same finite-only check allows an empty gweiFactor value to pass validation and produce a zero gas price instead of failing.
The Etherscan response parsing has the same issue as the non-Etherscan path: a null parameter value converts to 0 via Number(null) and passes validation instead of being flagged as missing.

The guard only checks Number.isFinite, but Number(''), Number('  ') and Number(null) all evaluate to 0, which is finite. An oracle response like { fast: '' }, { fast: null }, or FastGasPrice: '' therefore passes validation and is treated as a real gas price of 0n instead of being rejected as invalid.
The Etherscan parsing path can still produce a negative maxPriorityFeePerGas when suggestBaseFee exceeds FastGasPrice, and there is no bounds check enforcing a valid floor for this value.

The test builds a Chain object by hand with makeChain using an 'as unknown as Chain' cast instead of using the existing chainBuilder() builder already available in packages/utils/src/tests/builders/chains.ts, which bypasses the project's established builder/faker pattern for test data.

When data[gasParameter] is null, Number(null) evaluates to 0, which passes the Number.isFinite() check, so the code silently treats a missing oracle parameter as a valid zero value instead of raising an error.
The same sequence of steps (multiply by gweiFactor, check isFinite, throw, then BigInt(Math.round(...))) is duplicated three times across the file instead of being extracted into a shared helper.

The rounding tests should use inputs whose product is fractional, such as '22.8466851085' (which yields 22846685108.5), and assert a literal expected value like 22846685109n, so the tests would fail without correct rounding.
The test should use chainBuilder().with({ gasPrice, features }).build() and drop the unsafe type cast.

The expected values in the test are computed using the same BigInt(Math.round(x * 1e9)) expression used in the implementation, so the test merely restates the implementation rather than asserting an independent expected value.

The rounding test inputs (22.846685108*1e9, 20.123456789*1e9, 25.5*1e9) all multiply out to whole numbers, so removing Math.round from the implementation still leaves BigInt(...) working correctly and the tests still pass, meaning the float-to-BigInt rounding fix is not actually exercised by these tests.

The NaN-handling test block covers undefined, non-numeric strings, and a missing key, but has no test cases for empty string, whitespace-only string, or null, which are exactly the inputs that bypass the validation guard described in the source-code finding.

Because the invalid empty/null values are accepted rather than throwing, fetchGasOracle returns normally, so getGasPrice never falls back to the next oracle and getGasParameters never falls back to the provider feeData, causing the hook to report a fabricated price of 0 wei instead of signaling an unknown price.
Network calls in the test are mocked by directly replacing global.fetch instead of using MSW, which conflicts with the project's stated convention to use MSW instead of mocking fetch.

parseEtherscanOracleResult and the non-Etherscan numeric conversion are pure functions but are only exercised indirectly through renderHook with a mocked fetch, rather than being unit-tested directly.
The test computes its expected value using the same formula (BigInt(Math.round(value * 1e9))) that the code under test uses, so a rounding bug in the implementation would not be caught by the test.
